Welcome toPaddle Wheel in a Flow

A tiny paddle wheel floats in a flowing fluid: in which flows does it turn, and which way?

About: the curl of a flow in the plane as twice the mean rate at which two crossed lines of fluid start to turn

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the plane seen from above, x and y from −3 to 3 grid spacings at equal scales. Arrows on a 5 × 5 grid show v, centred on their points, with one length scale for all flows; dots mark points where v = 0. A paddle wheel with one coloured blade floats at its hub, with a line of fluid along x (blue, tagged x) and one along y (tagged y) crossing there; faint copies stay where they started. Right: the angle each line and the wheel have turned through against t.
Controls
Flow chooses the source, the rotation or the shear flow. Drag the wheel on the plane, or use the x0 and y0 sliders, to set where a run starts (each from −1.2 to 1.2 in steps of 0.1). Play runs 4 s of ordinary time; the picture then holds until you change a control, which returns the wheel to its start.
Measured
Every point of the lines and the hub is carried by the exact flow map eAt. The line rates are ∂vy/∂x and −∂vx/∂y at the starting point, the wheel's rate is half the z-component of the curl, all in units of 0.125 s−1, anticlockwise positive; they are listed in the Readouts panel under the controls and, in the guided inquiry, show dashes until a run at the current point and flow has ended.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The wheel in a rotating flow

Choose the rotation and leave the wheel at (1, 0). Before pressing play, predict what the wheel does as the fluid carries it round the centre.

2 · At the centre of the rotation

Keep the rotation and drag the wheel to the dot at the centre, (0, 0). Before pressing play, predict what the wheel does there.

3 · The wheel in a source flow

Choose the source flow and drag the wheel to (1, 0.5). Before pressing play, predict what the wheel and the two lines do.

4 · The wheel in a shear flow

Choose the shear flow and drag the wheel to (0, 1), in the upper rows, where the fluid moves to the right. Before pressing play, predict what the wheel does.

5 · Two crossed lines in the shear

Keep the shear flow and drag the wheel to (1, 0.5), also in the upper rows, so that the four rates show dashes again. Before pressing play and reading the four rates after the run, predict how the two lines of fluid start to turn.

6 · The lower rows of the shear

Keep the shear flow and drag the wheel to (0, −1), in the lower rows, where the fluid moves to the left. Before pressing play, predict what the wheel does.

7 · Summary

A paddle wheel turns at half the curl: the mean rate at which two crossed lines of fluid start to turn. The rotation flow has curl 2ω at every point, even at the centre where v = 0. The source flow spreads out (divergence 2k) but has zero curl, so nothing turns. The shear flow has straight streamlines yet curl −k, so the wheel turns clockwise at k/2 in every row. Curl measures local spin, not whether the flow goes round.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

The sim follows a small paddle wheel and two crossed lines of fluid while a steady flow carries them: a source, a rotation or a shear. The Readouts give the rate at which each line and the wheel start to turn, anticlockwise positive, in units of 0.125 s−1.

What you'll learn

  • How the turning of two crossed lines of fluid defines the curl.
  • How to get those rates from the velocity field with ∂vy/∂x and ∂vx/∂y.
  • What a rotation, a source and a shear each do to the lines and to the wheel.
  • How the answer changes, or does not, as the wheel starts elsewhere.
The sim's two views: the plane with the wheel and its two lines, and the angle turned against time.

What's on screen

  • Blue line: a line of fluid along x, tagged x. Its curve is blue on the plot.
  • Violet line: a line of fluid along y, tagged y, with a violet curve.
  • Orange blade: the paddle wheel at the hub of the two lines. Its curve is a dashed orange line.
  • Grey arrows: the velocity on a 5 × 5 grid, with one length scale for every flow. Dots mark points where v = 0.
  • Faint copies: the wheel and the lines where they started.
See itLook at the plane, the angle plot and the Readouts panel. Watch for: the wheel at (1, 0) with its two lines, and faint copies marking where they start.

03

Two crossed lines of fluid give the curl

Follow two short lines of fluid that start at one point, one of length Δx along x and one of length Δy along y (notes, section 3.1). The far end of the first moves in y faster than its near end by (∂vy/∂x) Δx, so that line turns anticlockwise at ∂vy/∂x. The far end of the second moves in x faster than its near end by (∂vx/∂y) Δy, which turns it clockwise, so its anticlockwise rate is −∂vx/∂y.

Each line turns because its far end is carried differently from its near end.
Eq. (3.15). The two line rates, and the wheel's rate, which is their mean.

A small paddle wheel with its axle along z turns at that mean rate, which is half the z-component of the curl. The result holds while the angles turned stay small. The sim's readouts are these rates at the start point.

See itOpen the Readouts panel and read the four rows. Watch for: the line along x, the line along y, their mean and the wheel, in units of 0.125 s⁻¹ with anticlockwise positive.
04

The rotation carries the wheel round and turns it at ω, even at the centre

In the rotation v = ω(−y, x), so ∂vy/∂x = ω and −∂vx/∂y = ω. Both lines turn at ω, so the wheel does too, and the curl is 2ω at every point.

The rotation, with ω = 0.125 s−1.
In the 4 s run the hub is carried 0.5 rad round the centre and the wheel turns through 0.5 rad.

Starting at (1, 0), the hub reaches (0.878, 0.479), 0.5 rad round the centre, and the wheel has turned through 0.5 rad, 28.6°, anticlockwise. It is not carried round while keeping its orientation. At the centre v = 0, so the hub stays where it is, yet the rates are the same and the wheel still turns 0.5 rad. The curl depends on how v changes across the wheel, not on the speed of the fluid.

See itChoose Rotation with the wheel at (1, 0) and press Play. Watch for: the hub carried round the centre while the wheel turns through the same angle, with all three rates reading 1.000.
05

The source lengthens the lines and turns nothing

In the source v = k(x, y), the field points away from the origin. Then ∂vy/∂x = 0 and ∂vx/∂y = 0 at every point, so neither line turns, and the curl is zero.

The source. Spreading out is the divergence, 2k here; it lengthens the lines.
The hub is carried outward and both lines lengthen, while the blade keeps its angle.

What the source does is stretch. A line of fluid along x grows as ekt, so after 4 s, with kt = 0.5, it is 1.65 times as long. A wheel started at (1, 0.5) is carried out to (1.65, 0.82) and its angle is still zero. Spreading out is the divergence; turning is the curl; the source has the first without the second.

See itChoose Source, put the wheel at (1, 0.5) and press Play. Watch for: the wheel carried outward and both lines lengthening, with the wheel and the line angles staying at zero.
06

The shear turns the wheel although every streamline is straight

In the shear v = k(y, 0) the fluid above the x-axis moves right and the fluid below it moves left, faster the further from the axis. One might think that fluid moving along straight lines does not rotate, but the notes show otherwise (section 3.1).

The shear, with k = 0.125 s−1.
The line along x does not tilt. The line along y tilts clockwise, and the wheel turns clockwise in the upper row and in the lower row alike.

The line along x does not turn. The line along y does, clockwise at k, because its upper end is carried faster than its lower end. The wheel takes the mean, −k/2. From (0, 1) the hub moves right to (0.5, 1) in 4 s, and the wheel turns 0.25 rad, 14.3°, clockwise.

See itChoose Shear, put the wheel at (0, 1) and press Play. Watch for: the wheel turning clockwise although every arrow is horizontal, with the x-line rate 0.000 and the y-line rate −1.000.
07

The wheel's rate is the same at every point of each flow

The rates in units of 0.125 s−1, anticlockwise positive, are these, wherever the wheel starts:

FlowLine along xLine along yWheelCurl z
Rotation1.0001.0001.0002.000
Source0.0000.0000.0000.000
Shear0.000−1.000−0.500−1.000

Each flow is linear in x and y, so ∂vy/∂x and ∂vx/∂y are constants. The rotation's rates are the same at the centre as at (1, 0). The shear's are the same in the upper rows, where the fluid moves right, as in the lower rows, where it moves left, since the row below moves left faster. Changing x0 or y0 changes the speed at the hub, which the arrows show, and leaves the four rates alone.

See itVisit three starts in turn: the rotation at (0, 0), the shear at (0, −1), the source at (−1.2, 1.2). Watch for: the four rows matching the table at each, and the wheel reading −0.500 in the lower row of the shear.
08

Where it matters

  • Spin of a flow. The z-component of the curl is twice the mean angular velocity of the fluid about the z-axis near the point (notes, section 3.1). A wheel in the fluid turns at half the curl.
  • A gradient has no curl. ∇ × (∇f) = 0 (3.16), so the field of a point charge has zero curl wherever it is defined. A field with curl, such as the rotation, cannot be a gradient.
  • Spreading is not turning. The divergence measures how a small volume grows, the curl how it turns. The source has one, the rotation and the shear the other.
Go deeper: the angles in the plot are not all small

Eq. (3.15) gives rates at the start, valid while the turned angles stay small. In the 4 s run the shear's y-line turns by θy = −tan−1(kt), with kt = 0.5, which is −26.6°, not the −28.6° that a constant rate k would give. The x-line stays at 0, and the wheel's curve, with its constant rate −k/2, reaches −0.25 rad.

The finite turn of the y-line in the shear.
09

Summary

In one line. The curl at a point is twice the mean rate at which two crossed short lines of fluid start to turn, and a small paddle wheel turns at half the curl.
  • Rotation v = ω(−y, x): both lines and the wheel turn at ω everywhere, the curl is 2ω, even at the centre where v = 0.
  • Source v = k(x, y): the lines lengthen, nothing turns, and the curl is zero.
  • Shear v = k(y, 0): straight streamlines, yet the wheel turns clockwise at k/2 in every row, and the curl is −k.

Common mix-ups

  • "Straight streamlines mean no curl." The shear has straight streamlines and curl −k.
  • "A slow fluid turns the wheel slowly." At the centre of the rotation v = 0 and the wheel still turns at ω.
  • "A fluid that spreads out is turning." The source has divergence 2k and curl zero.

Things to try on your own

  • Shear with the wheel at (1, 0.5): the x-line reads 0.000, the y-line −1.000 and the wheel −0.500.
  • Rotation at (0, 0): after a run the angle plot shows 0.5 rad at 4 s while the hub has not moved.
  • Source at (−1.2, 1.2): after a run the lines are 1.65 times longer and nothing has turned.
